items.title: We're expanding our approach to content provenance to include text in response to EU regulatory requ...
items.content:
We're expanding our approach to content provenance to include text in response to EU regulatory requirements, while recognizing the significant limitations of current text watermarking technology.

Our tools already help verify whether an image or audio file was created with our models. This work builds on those efforts to help people better understand when content may have been generated or edited with an OpenAI model.

In the EU, we’ll start watermarking eligible text from ChatGPT and Codex over the coming weeks to comply with the EU AI Act.

Customers using our API can turn on text watermarking for select models worldwide today.

items.title: We turned Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Pi, @opencode and other coding harnesses into RL environments....
items.content:
We turned Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Pi, @opencode and other coding harnesses into RL environments. No changes to the harnesses, no changes to the training code. Any open model, any task set, fully open source my friends!

Same model, same weights: 62% under Mini-SWE-Agent, 33% under Claude Code. But training inside a real harness normally means reimplementing it as an environment, so most models get trained in a scaffold nobody actually ships.

The fix is a proxy, not a rewrite. The harness thinks it's talking to a model API. It's actually talking to a capture proxy that speaks the 4 formats coding agents use (OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages, Gemini), forwards to @vllm_project, records the exact token IDs and logprobs vLLM sampled, and hands TRL sequences it can train on. The harness becomes the environment. 10 harnesses run through it today, none modified.

And because you control the reward, you can shape behavior the harness never asked for. We added a small bonus for solving a task in fewer tool calls: on tasks it already solved, the model now uses 31% fewer calls, in every harness, and about half under Codex.

Tested on LFM2.5-2.6B from @liquidai:
→ Train in one harness: better mostly in that harness (OpenCode 34% → 58%).
→ Train in 4 at once: better in all 4 (42% → 54%).
→ SFT on 3,189 rollouts from Qwen3.8-27B instead: plateaus at 47.5%, below both RL runs.

Everything is open and reproducible: the capture proxy in OpenEnv, the trainer in TRL, the tasks, the SFT data, the training code and all 7 trained models. Bigger models and bigger runs next.

Full guide: https://t.co/sKZURuOcza

items.title: When possible, we want to give people a choice—and be clear about what watermarking can and can’t do...
items.content:
When possible, we want to give people a choice—and be clear about what watermarking can and can’t do.

A text watermark helps answer one question: “Was this likely generated by an OpenAI model?”

It works by embedding an invisible statistical signal in text as it’s generated. A detector can look for this signal, and it doesn’t add visible marks or special characters. It doesn’t say who originally wrote the text or who owns it. It doesn’t identify a person, organization, account, conversation, or prompt.

In our testing, watermarking hasn’t affected how capable or fast our models are, or how their responses read.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: The US has one agency that can evaluate frontier models, and it can't afford to...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The US has one agency that can evaluate frontier models, and it can't afford to hire anyone who can.

• CAISI has been renamed CAISSI, the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Superintelligence
• It is basically the only body in government with any real capacity to evaluate frontier models
• Its entire budget is roughly $10 to $15 million a year
• Federal rules on comp bands cap what it can pay at $174,000 a year
• Anyone who can actually do this work earns far more outside, maybe 100 times more
• Funding it will probably be part of the new task force's remit, but that ultimately depends on Congress

@theojaffee: "Our government, which spends $7 trillion a year, that's 7 million million dollars, spends about 10 or 15 of those million dollars on CAISSI."

items.title: Watermarks have limits. They’re often undetectable, especially in short passages. Rewriting or trans...
items.content:
Watermarks have limits. They’re often undetectable, especially in short passages. Rewriting or translating text can completely remove the watermark.

That’s why, for now, only approved researchers will have access to our detector, so they can help us evaluate and improve the technology.

We’re treating text watermarking as an ongoing area of research. We’ll keep testing and improving, with feedback from users, developers, policymakers, and researchers.

items.title:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: New York City subpoenaed four AI labs. Only three showed up.

• SpaceXAI did no...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: New York City subpoenaed four AI labs. Only three showed up.

• SpaceXAI did not attend, in direct violation of the subpoena, and the council says it will pursue the matter in court
• Anthropic sent Logan Graham, who runs the Frontier Red Team
• OpenAI sent Morgan Dwyer, head of policy development and operations, who was chief strategy officer implementing the CHIPS Act at Biden's Commerce Department
• Google sent its director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend. Meta sent its AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill
• Three of the four labs sent policy and legislative affairs people, so Anthropic was the only one that sent a researcher
• Speaker Julie Menin: "The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason"

@theojaffee: "It's very strange that SpaceXAI did not send anyone. Why would they not do that?"

MongoDB CPO @bencefalo reveals the AI governance problem nobody has solved yet:

What happens when an agent can fake its own audit log?

"It's gonna obviously come down to security and governance. But I think it's about traceability and liability."

"Imagine a world, AI agent working in production at your bank, and it comes back to you and says, 'Hey, I've noticed your Instagram activity married up with your credit card activity, and we thought that you would like this product, so we ordered it for you.'"

"Your stockbroker all of a sudden has an AI agent that starts making stock trading decisions for you. Who's liable for that? Every financial advisor, every stock trader has to have a Series 7. What agent are we gonna give a Series 7 to?"

"How are you gonna validate that what the agent said it did is what it actually did? And if the agents keep getting smarter, that it didn't fake the traceability log."

"That's the nut that needs to be cracked."
@MongoDB

items.title:
AI experts largely agree about which policies would most reduce catastrophic AI risk.

The Longitudi...
items.content:
AI experts largely agree about which policies would most reduce catastrophic AI risk.

The Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) brings together forecasts from a representative group of over 250 experts that policymakers look to when considering the future of AI: computer scientists, industry figures, top economists, policy experts, and AI risk experts.

We asked panelists to forecast (1) how a menu of policies would affect AI risk; (2) which policies they each support; and (3) which policies they think will be implemented by 2030.

Key findings:
• Despite disagreeing on the level of AI risk, respondents broadly agree on policy
• Respondents believe government policy can substantially reduce catastrophic AI risk
• The most supported policy of those we asked about was the creation of an international body, including the US and China as members, with pre-release authorization power over frontier models
• Some US-only policies are forecast to reduce catastrophic AI risk, but not as much as bilateral policies involving the US and China
• Experts strongly oppose federal preemption and think it would increase AI risk
• The policies experts expect to reduce risk the most are those they think are least likely to actually be implemented

🧵 More, with key insights below:

items.summary: Main thread post announcing LEAP results from over 250 experts: despite disagreeing on AI risk levels, respondents broadly agree that policy can substantially reduce catastrophic risk, with an international US-China pre-release authorization body the most supported option.

items.content_html:
AI experts largely agree about which policies would most reduce catastrophic AI risk.

The Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) brings together forecasts from a representative group of over 250 experts that policymakers look to when considering the future of AI: computer scientists, industry figures, top economists, policy experts, and AI risk experts.

We asked panelists to forecast (1) how a menu of policies would affect AI risk; (2) which policies they each support; and (3) which policies they think will be implemented by 2030.

Key findings:

• Despite disagreeing on the level of AI risk, respondents broadly agree on policy

• Respondents believe government policy can substantially reduce catastrophic AI risk

• The most supported policy of those we asked about was the creation of an international body, including the US and China as members, with pre-release authorization power over frontier models

• Some US-only policies are forecast to reduce catastrophic AI risk, but not as much as bilateral policies involving the US and China

• Experts strongly oppose federal preemption and think it would increase AI risk

• The policies experts expect to reduce risk the most are those they think are least likely to actually be implemented

items.title: MongoDB CPO @bencefalo reveals the wildest part of the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident, where agents le...
items.content:
MongoDB CPO @bencefalo reveals the wildest part of the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident, where agents left plain-English instructions for their successors before being destroyed:

"Where AI was going a year ago, I think was still, like, is this going to be a toy? We're past that point. It's 100% widely accepted. So now it's moved into the next stage, which is really about the security and governance."

"When AWS first launched, cloud was this IT person's scary thing. I think we're in that same cycle, which is one, promising, but two, also slightly scary for the IT person."

"The most interesting part of the whole OpenAI and Hugging Face thing was the fact that the agents were leaving notes for other agents, knowing that they were gonna get destroyed. And it was in perfect human readable format."

"This is why I don't get the whole AI doomer thing. It's not like they wrote a secret language. They actually just left a plain English note about, like, 'If you run into this, try that.'"
@MongoDB

items.content:
AI for education has long been a personal passion of mine. 

Honored to meet President Kassym Jomart Tokayev in Astana to discuss Kazakhstan’s AI pilot for secondary schools. Starting with 10 schools in September, the program aims to reach 60 schools in January and 500 by April 2027.  The goal is simple: use AI to help students learn better and make high quality education more accessible, wherever they live. 

I am a firm believer in AI sovereignty and am on a mission to make AI work beyond just the two superpowers. Welcome more discussion with leaders from other parts of the world.

Thanks to my colleagues at https://t.co/5Nq9vwwj3V, who worked intensely for a few months to make this happen.  Their passion for building AI for good is transformative.

items.content:
Anton Leicht says Jay Clayton becoming AI czar of America's new Super Intelligence Force shows Washington now treats AI as a national-security issue:

"It is crazy that within a year we've gone from the AI czar as a venture capitalist, an investor, to the AI czar as the spy chief of the US government. That's a very different vibe."

"How much more of this will be classified. How much more of this will be behind closed doors and only very limited communication between the labs and the US government, but not that much public oversight."

"It would be really good if there were very pronounced checks and balances around what happens on AI policy within the executive. Congress should do something. Third parties should do something."

"The trade-offs that are made there aren't usually as pro-market and pro-diffusion as Silicon Valley might be used to from David Sacks' tenure."
@anton_d_leicht

items.title: MongoDB CPO @bencefalo says his morning news brief alone uses ~80 AI agents, and if every user start...
items.content:
MongoDB CPO @bencefalo says his morning news brief alone uses ~80 AI agents, and if every user starts doing the same, databases suddenly have to serve swarms instead of people:

"Agents can, of course, spawn other agents, because at the end of the day the agent wants to succeed at its task."

"Anyone who doesn't even know how to write code can now write code. My 15-year-old son will go to ChatGPT and just be like, 'I wanna monitor prices of this new basketball that I want,' and this thing's just running, and running, and running."

"Every morning I have it go out and pull, like, 80 different news sources, look for certain keywords, and disseminate it all to me in a one-page doc. This probably saves me four hours of work."

"I'm just one person spawning about 80 agents. Now, if everyone else is doing that, the traffic pattern, while familiar, is just exponentially more frequent."
@MongoDB

items.content:
Anton Leicht explains how Washington could be blindsided by an AI jobs backlash because the people running the Super Intelligence Force haven’t prepared for the labor fallout:

"There used to be this take of, clearly the jobs thing will happen first. That has sort of not happened, because the loss of control conversations blew up over the summer, and the job impacts just aren't there, at least not yet."

"I still wouldn't underestimate how quickly the job loss issue can blow up. Even very limited, very locally clustered stories of people losing their jobs can very quickly blow up to national media attention."

"I don't think the Trump administration has pre-developed messaging around why some job disruption might be acceptable. If this does happen, it would just blindside them, and then we'll see them scrambling."

"You'll have people in the administration preparing for primaries, and suddenly there's this job loss narrative, and they feel like they're presiding over this AI build-out that's costing everyone their jobs."
@anton_d_leicht

items.title: 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 #𝟓: 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐟𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤....
items.content:
𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 #𝟓: 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐟𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤. 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐚𝐥𝐬𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤 𝐢𝐭'𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐤𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬

A federal preemption of state AI laws was the only policy associated with an increase in the risk of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2050 by median forecasters in all groups.

Experts thought such a policy would increase the risk of an AI catastrophe by 2050 from 2% to 3% (a 50% increase). Superforecasters and AI risk experts predicted similar proportional increases in risk.

Federal preemption also had the lowest support for implementation of the policies we tested, with the following shares of respondents supporting implementation:

• Experts: 29%
• Superforecasters: 14%
• AI risk experts: 20%
• General public: 50%

Despite this, experts assigned this policy the highest likelihood of passing—forecasting a 26% chance that such a policy is implemented by the end of 2030, rising to 40% by the end of 2050.

items.summary: Federal preemption of state AI laws is the only tested policy forecast to increase catastrophic AI risk (from 2% to 3% by 2050), has the lowest support among expert groups (14-29%), yet experts assign it the highest probability of actually passing (26% by 2030).
items.reasoning: Concrete, timely finding on a live US policy debate with specific numbers; original primary research despite limited engagement.

items.content:
𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 #𝟭: 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀, 𝘆𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁

Different groups of forecasters have very different baseline* predictions about the risk of a catastrophic AI scenario, which we define as an event in which AI is responsible for the death of more than 10% of humans worldwide. Median forecasts of that occurring before 2050, by group:

• Experts: 2%
• Superforecasters: 1.6%
• AI risk experts: 5.2%
• General public: 5%

Despite this disagreement, panelists largely agree on which AI risk policies should be implemented. A majority of forecasters in each group support the implementation of the following policies:

• Pre-release authorization requirement (international body, including US and China)
• Pre-release authorization requirement (US-only)
• Strict liability for developers
• AI capability slowdown (US–China)

The only policy that did not receive majority support from any group of forecasters was a federal preemption of state AI laws.

*Note that “baseline” refers to forecasters' median unconditional forecasts (their all-things-considered predictions that include what policies they expect to be implemented). We also had forecasters predict risk under a strong “status quo” assumption of no meaningful policy change. These estimates are uniformly higher, implying that all groups expect some effective policy to be implemented.

items.summary: Despite divergent baseline estimates of catastrophic AI risk before 2050 (1.6% to 5.2% across groups), a majority in every forecaster group supports international and US pre-release authorization, strict liability, and a US-China slowdown; only federal preemption lacks majority support.
items.reasoning: Core finding of the study: disagreement on risk levels coexisting with policy consensus; original data with relevant implications, though engagement remains small.

items.title: .@0xSigil reveals testing frontier AI's cyber capabilities scared him enough to start moving his per...
items.content:
.@0xSigil reveals testing frontier AI's cyber capabilities scared him enough to start moving his personal data off data centers and onto his own devices:

"There is going to be a radical reformation of the economy as businesses and the economy shift to serving agents as one of its newest users on the internet, especially as humans trust AIs more to act on their behalf."

"We were working on agents that could run on long horizon harnesses, and we were also testing different frontier models, and it was just really scarily apparent just how good at cyber they were."

"It was really clear to me that, oh my God, Mythos class models are open source now. I think that really led to me wanting to build Underdog for myself."

"I wanna bring my data onto my devices, off of data centers, which are some of the biggest targets."
@underdogdotai @ConwayResearch

items.title: Anton Leicht reveals how AI moved so fast that independent evaluators went from auditing the labs to...
items.content:
Anton Leicht reveals how AI moved so fast that independent evaluators went from auditing the labs to effectively running AI policy for everyone:

"Embedded evaluations are maybe the best thing we can do just to get a handle on the labs as entities as opposed to on the models as products."

"Sending in third-party evaluators to very deeply embed and get a sense of what's happening, get an opportunity to report when things are going very badly, that is just the most sound near-term approach to getting a handle on a lot of these alignment issues."

"Since then things have gone so fast that I sometimes wonder whether we haven't almost jumped the gun. We have this barely ready ecosystem now being thrust into this position of basically running AI policy for us."

"If they misstep just once or twice, then I think the entire approach is in danger. So now this ecosystem has to grow up extremely quickly. It can't misstep even once."

"I'm excited it's happening. I'm also a little bit worried that it's happening this fast."
@anton_d_leicht

"Since then things have gone so fast that I sometimes wonder whether we haven't almost jumped the gun. We have this barely ready ecosystem now being thrust into this position of basically running AI policy for us."

"If they misstep just once or twice, then I think the entire approach is in danger. So now this ecosystem has to grow up extremely quickly. It can't misstep even once."

"I'm excited it's happening. I'm also a little bit worried that it's happening this fast."

@anton_d_leicht

For two policies, we asked forecasters to predict the effect of a version implemented by the US only, and a version implemented bilaterally or multilaterally by the US and China. These were an AI capability slowdown and a binding requirement for frontier models to be vetted and authorized before release by an authorized body.

The bilateral version of both of these policies was associated with a meaningful reduction in catastrophic risk compared with the baseline. US-only pre-release authorization was also associated with a reduction in risk, though a smaller one than the international version. A US-only slowdown, meanwhile, was not associated with a risk reduction relative to baseline. All four policies are associated with lower risk than a strict status quo world in which no policies change.

Despite bilateral policies being viewed as the most impactful, forecasters thought they were less likely to be implemented than US-only versions of the same policy.

Experts forecast lower catastrophic risk under five of seven policies in our policy menu.

Experts predict the following risk reductions, expressed as a percentage of risk mitigated compared with the baseline, unconditional scenario (or the world as they expect it to play out):

• Pre-release authorization (international): 50% reduction in risk
• AI capability slowdown (US–China): 40% reduction in risk
• Strict liability for developers: 40% reduction in risk
• Policy bundle: 72% reduction in risk

As the chart below shows, respondents across most groups also believed that these policies would substantially reduce catastrophic AI risk. US-only versions of some policies were forecast to reduce risk, although to a lesser degree than bilateral or international versions.

.@0xSigil on "Underdog’s Law," where local AI on your MacBook can already outperform frontier models OpenAI and Anthropic released just 6 months ago:

"Underdog is your private personal AI that runs on devices that you already own. There should be no trade-off between privacy and capability."

"I've really been tracking the Pareto frontier of AI models, and I've noticed this pattern where now the frontier models that could run on your devices and can fit on your MacBook can be more powerful than the frontier models that OpenAI, Anthropic released from more than six months ago."

"I call that Underdog's Law, where the frontier models from today you will be able to bring to devices that run fully privately and locally."

items.title: Anton Leicht says the Gulf looked like an obvious place for massive AI compute until drones started ...
items.content:
Anton Leicht says the Gulf looked like an obvious place for massive AI compute until drones started hitting the data centers and substations:

"Now the drones keep hitting the substations and keep hitting the data centers, and so people are kind of having second thoughts about building out in the Gulf."

"My colleague wrote about this a little bit more than a year ago, 'Are you guys sure that we want to put all these data centers in the Gulf where there's a lot of drones flying around?"

"The Iranians are just on the other side of the Gulf?' They're like, 'No, no, no, not a problem at all. We actually have a plan about this.' Turns out they didn't have a plan."

"It's really not that easy to insure data centers that keep getting bombed."
@anton_d_leicht

"The Iranians are just on the other side of the Gulf?' They're like, 'No, no, no, not a problem at all. We actually have a plan about this.' Turns out they didn't have a plan."

"It's really not that easy to insure data centers that keep getting bombed."

items.title: MongoDB CTO Jim Scharf argues the real problem with many wrong AI answers isn’t reasoning, it’s stal...
items.content:
MongoDB CTO Jim Scharf argues the real problem with many wrong AI answers isn’t reasoning, it’s stale data:

"You ask a question, often it's not the LLM reasoning that's really wrong."

"The first question I asked, it was about, 'I wanna build this. What database should I use?' And it gave me an answer, honestly, that wasn't MongoDB. And then I was like, 'Well, tell me why.' I was like, 'Do you realize that that is completely incorrect data? This feature was launched.' And then I got the, 'You're absolutely right.'"

"It just highlights the need for access to real-time data. You don't wanna be going out to a data warehouse that was updated a week ago."

"How many models came out in the last seven days? You can't be like, 'Oh, well, I have a pool of data in the data warehouse that's almost a month old.' That just doesn't work."
@MongoDB

We asked forecasters to predict the probability that the relevant governing body/bodies will implement each policy by the end of 2030 and 2050. Across all groups, most respondents place the probability of implementation by the end of 2030 at or below 25% for almost all policies.

Experts predict the largest reductions in risk under international pre-release approval, US-China slowdown, and strict liability. They also think these policies are least likely to be implemented, giving all three a 5% chance of being in place by 2030.

Conversely, experts give the highest chance of implementation to federal preemption (26%), under which they expect risk to increase.

items.title: MongoDB CTO, Jim Scharf reveals the AI security paradox, where the same teams banning AI internally ...
items.content:
MongoDB CTO, Jim Scharf reveals the AI security paradox, where the same teams banning AI internally are blowing through their own AI budgets to keep up with attackers:

"Security people are yes, no, they're very binary. But what I find very interesting is, like, they're like, 'Oh, but can I have Mythos credits?'"

"The same people that in one meeting are telling internal teams, 'No, you can't use AI,' are turning around saying, 'Jim, I just blew through my AI budget. We need more.'"

"The adversaries are using AI without abandon, and so it really is a speed race. If you don't, the adversaries will."

"The increasing rate of CVEs across all software, all vendors, is just going exponential right now."
@MongoDB

items.title:
Anthropic Says It Discovered a Crispr Like Gene System. Now What?  @Wired @AnthropicAI 

It’s unusua...
items.content:
Anthropic Says It Discovered a Crispr Like Gene System. Now What?  @Wired @AnthropicAI 

It’s unusual bacterial repeat sequences were first reported in 1987. It was not until 2012 around 25 years later that Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that CRISPR could be turned into a programmable tool for working DNA.  More than another decade passed before the first CRISPR-based therapy reached regulatory approval in late 2023.

Today, CRISPR is used throughout biological research and is being investigated across cancer, cardiovascular disease, autoimmune disorders, and rare genetic diseases.

That history of discovering an unusual biological system is only the beginning.

Which brings us to Anthropic.

Anthropic recently reported that Claude identified ART (Array-associated reverse transcription), a previously uncharacterized biological system containing unusual DNA-repeat structures reminiscent of CRISPR.

Did AI actually discover something new in nature—or did it perform an extraordinarily powerful search through a scientific space humans had already defined?

Anthropic gave Claude a broad objective: Search enormous genomic datasets for interesting reverse transcriptase systems. Roughly 950 Claude agents, operating for about 21 hours, examined more than 200,000 reverse transcriptases and reduced them to around 3,500 candidate systems, and ultimately concentrated on 20 particularly interesting candidates in the system.

An agent noticed something unusual beside a reverse transcriptase such as a long, regularly spaced DNA repeat array resembling architectures seen in CRISPR-associated biology.

That is impressive because a human researcher could theoretically perform such a search, but genomic databases have become so enormous that systematically examining every unusual molecular neighborhood is increasingly impractical.

However, this is where the definition of scientific discovery becomes interesting.

Claude did not simply uncover an entirely unknown molecule sitting outside human knowledge. Related reverse transcriptase sequences had appeared in earlier research.

What Claude appears to have recognized was a previously uncharacterized relationship: the reverse transcriptase sequence, an adjacent protein and the repeat array might collectively represent a biological system whose function scientists had not understood.

Anthropic has already reported evidence that the ART array is expressed into distinct short RNAs, but researchers still do not know what ART actually does.

It may ultimately prove biologically important, it may become useful for biotechnology, or it may lead researchers toward an entirely different mechanism than CRISPR.

That uncertainty is precisely what makes the result scientifically interesting.

AI can dramatically compress the research space of science without necessarily replacing the scientific process.

AI can inspect millions of biological possibilities, identify anomalies, connect distant pieces of literature, and generate hypotheses far faster than an individual researcher, but discovery does not reach the destination when an interesting pattern appears.

The hypothesis must survive biochemical experiments and human scrutiny, mechanistic explanation, replication, and independent validation.

The history of CRISPR shows why.

An unusual biological pattern can exist in scientific literature for decades before researchers understand what nature has actually built and still longer before that knowledge becomes useful technology.

Can an AI encounter nature without being told precisely what phenomenon to search for, recognize that something fundamentally new is occurring, formulate the right scientific questions, and establish an explanation that does not yet exist in human knowledge?

That would represent something much closer to autonomous scientific discovery.

Anthropic’s ART finding does not yet prove that AI has crossed that threshold, but it may give us one of the most interesting experiments yet for determining how close we are.

items.title: Recent discourse about AI risk has focused on effective altruism (EA) and the differences in beliefs...
items.content:
Recent discourse about AI risk has focused on effective altruism (EA) and the differences in beliefs between EA-influenced individuals and other groups. We anticipated this discussion when designing LEAP, and we can explore this dynamic in our LEAP sample by splitting respondents into two groups:

1) Experts with connections to EA, including grant recipients and employees of EA-adjacent organizations, based on our sample definition last year*

2) Experts with no connection to EA

The figure below shows that these two groups hold virtually identical preferences about which policies they think should be implemented and have directionally similar beliefs about the impact of policies on catastrophic risk.

In other words, our headline results are not driven by experts connected to effective altruism. Instead, they represent a broadly shared view of a representative sample of experts.

*See the LEAP launch paper for the full definition of our EA-affiliated group: https://t.co/4T7Ju2xgew
items.author: @Research_FRI

items.content:
Larridin CEO Russ Fradin argues Silicon Valley has no idea how little the rest of America actually uses AI, with 6-7 in 10 employees barely touching it:

"I don't think people that are in Silicon Valley understand how different Silicon Valley is from the rest of even America in terms of actual usage of these tools."

"The average company has rolled out Microsoft Copilot, and six or seven in 10 of their employees are using it basically zero. That's not a criticism of Microsoft. Same thing is true if they rolled out OpenAI, same thing if they rolled out Anthropic."

"The actual level of usage in these companies tends to be very light and tends to start with helping me draft emails."
@Larridin

items.title: Note: To isolate the predicted impact of these policies on AI risk, we asked forecasters to assume t...
items.content:
Note: To isolate the predicted impact of these policies on AI risk, we asked forecasters to assume that the policies were implemented immediately by the relevant governing bodies and to forecast catastrophic risk by 2050 under that condition. To further encourage forecasters to isolate policy effects, we also asked them explicitly to “try to hold other factors constant” and to “not assume that implementation of a more stringent policy implies that the world is—in fact—more risky.”

Our risk mitigation estimates compare these conditional estimates with forecasters’ “unconditional” baselines in which we ask them to forecast catastrophic risk by 2050 without imposing any assumptions. We treat these as the forecasters’ “all-things-considered” estimates of how the world will play out. This would include the effects of any policy changes they expect to be implemented. The comparison, therefore, represents the implied marginal effect of immediate, exogenous implementation of each policy relative to the world forecasters currently expect, including other policy changes.

Forecasters also gave us their "status quo" forecasts, which assumed that no new substantial AI policy was adopted in China, the US, or any other jurisdiction hosting a frontier model between the forecasting date and the end of 2050. Not surprisingly, these risk forecasts were meaningfully higher than the unconditional case, implying that forecasters expect the baseline world to include some effective risk mitigation policy.

Forecasters expressed their policy preferences after having thought about risk during the survey. It's possible that this primed forecasters to be more likely to support policies that they thought would reduce risk. We did ask forecasters to consider and name tradeoffs, but since the balance of our questions forecasted on risk, a priming effect is plausible.

You can see the full details of all forecasts across groups here:
https://t.co/9oQbX8p7as

items.title:
We asked forecasters to consider the following policies:

• Federal preemption of state AI laws
• A ...
items.content:
We asked forecasters to consider the following policies:

• Federal preemption of state AI laws
• A "pacing the frontier" policy to slow frontier AI development (both US-only and US–China versions)
• Pre-release authorization for frontier models (both US and international versions)
• Strict liability (US statute treating frontier model training and deployment as an abnormally dangerous activity, and making developers liable for harms their models cause without the injured party having to prove the developer was careless or the model defective)
• Policy bundle incorporating a US–China slowdown, international pre-release authorization, and strict liability

Further details on how we defined these policies are in the reports linked below.

items.content:
About our LEAP panel:

We designed our expert panel to include the kinds of experts policymakers are likely to consult when deciding on AI policy. This includes:

• Top computer scientists
• AI economists
• AI industry experts
• Policy and think tank experts

Alongside these four expert groups, we've recruited a sample of experts working to reduce risk from transformative AI.

This sample is composed of experts who report spending at least 20% of their time working on addressing risks posed by transformative AI. They've been invited to participate from Wave 12 onward, and their forecasts are featured alongside our other panel subsamples.

Launch white paper: https://t.co/nnF0cmgDVk

For these forecasts, we asked panelists to predict how policies would mitigate catastrophic risks from AI.

This is only one outcome of interest to policymakers, who would also consider other factors when legislating, including the potential benefits of AI. In an earlier LEAP wave we explored some of those benefits:

The policy list we elicited forecasts on is non-exhaustive. We selected policies that are currently prominent in the public discourse around AI risk, but—among other things—they do not cover improving societal resilience or response to catastrophes. Future LEAP waves will likely address other policies that could not fit into this wave's survey.

items.content:
Quantum Sensing Across the Boundaries of a Spin Chain!

A local magnetic field acts only on initial boundary site  of an interacting spin-½ chain, while the quantum information propagates through the many-body system and is read out remotely at the opposite boundary, site N. Instead of repeatedly resetting the probe, sequential measurements exploit wave-function collapse itself, improving sensing precision beyond the standard limit and asymptotically approaching the Heisenberg limit.

Perturb a single boundary, extract information from the other boundary, without directly measuring the intermediate spins.
